slides.title: Amenability As Coarse Averaging
slides.notes: Open by making amenability sound like a compatibility problem for averaging, not a mysterious label. The chapter asks whether group motion can preserve a notion of mean, and the lecture will keep translating that question into finite boundary tests that students can inspect.

slides.title: Invariant Means
slides.notes: Pause on the mean because it is intentionally abstract. Students should hear positivity, normalization, and translation invariance as the three permissions that make an average behave globally. The orbit diagram reminds them that moving every input by a group element should not change the reported value.

slides.title: From Means To Finite Witnesses
slides.notes: Use this slide as the conceptual bridge from functional analysis to finite geometry. A Folner set is not exactly invariant; it is mostly unchanged after each generator move. The overlap picture lets students see approximate invariance before the boundary formula appears.

slides.title: Boundary Divided By Volume
slides.notes: Define the boundary operationally in a Cayley graph: generator steps that leave the chosen finite set. The ratio is the inspection target because it separates temporary edge effects from asymptotic behavior. A good sequence makes the escaping part negligible compared with the whole region.

slides.title: Folner Sequences In Lattices
slides.notes: Make the lattice example feel almost physical. Large intervals or squares have a surface layer that grows slower than the interior, so small translations disturb only a thin rim. This gives students the first durable mental model for why abelian groups are amenable.

slides.title: Checked Ratios For Z2
slides.notes: Treat the notebook figure as evidence with a visible audit trail. The sampled square ratios decrease from about 1.33 to about 0.21, and the saved check records that monotone trend. The exact numbers matter less than the stable pattern: boundary growth loses to area growth.

slides.title: Free Groups Keep A Frontier
slides.notes: Contrast the lattice picture with branching. In the free tree, a ball acquires many new outward edges whenever the radius grows, so most of the visual attention stays near the frontier. The notebook check reports ratios staying near six rather than drifting toward zero.

slides.title: Paradoxical Decomposition Signal
slides.notes: Present paradoxical decomposition as the opposite of a stable average. If finitely many pieces can be shifted into two full-looking copies, then a translation-invariant normalized mean would have to assign incompatible sizes. The diagram is schematic and original; it illustrates the counting pressure, not a source figure.

slides.title: Tarski Equivalence Compass
slides.notes: Use the compass slide to organize the equivalent faces without proving every implication. The class should leave knowing which statements are analytic, finite-combinatorial, and geometric. The lecture spends most time on Folner witnesses because they connect directly to Cayley graph inspection.

slides.title: Examples And Nonexamples
slides.notes: Read the table as a calibration device. Finite, abelian, and solvable groups support averaging behavior, while a free subgroup of rank two is a strong nonamenability witness. Also mention that the converse is delicate, so the table is a guide rather than a classification theorem.

slides.title: Closure Moves
slides.notes: Amenability becomes usable because it survives common algebraic constructions. Quotients, subgroups, extensions, and directed unions can carry the property in controlled ways. The point of the diagram is strategic: once a group is built from known amenable pieces, a new boundary experiment is often unnecessary.

slides.title: Quasi-Isometry Invariance
slides.notes: Frame quasi-isometry invariance as the chapter's coarse-geometry payoff. For finitely generated groups, a rough equivalence distorts distances by bounded multiplicative and additive errors, but it does not turn vanishing boundary ratios into persistent frontiers. The thickened-image diagram shows why finite noise can be absorbed.

slides.title: Shape Noise Versus Asymptotic Signal
slides.notes: Connect the applied lab to the theorem habit. Boxes, diamonds, and random connected regions may have different early ratios, but a successful family eventually suppresses boundary relative to volume. This is the same discipline as quasi-isometry: ignore bounded presentation choices and track asymptotic evidence.

slides.title: Proof Roadmap For Coarse Transfer
slides.notes: Give students a proof map instead of a full technical proof. Start with a good finite set, move it across a quasi-isometry, thicken to repair holes, and compare boundary and volume using bounded geometry. Each step has a reason, and each reason is visible in the pipeline.

slides.title: Classroom Lab
slides.notes: Turn the chapter into a reproducible experiment. Ask groups to choose a generating set, propose a growing family, compute its boundary ratio, and predict the limit before plotting. The final check should record both the numerical trend and the mathematical invariant the trend is meant to test.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the original question about averaging. Means are the invariant ideal, Folner sequences are finite witnesses, paradoxical decompositions are the obstruction, and quasi-isometry invariance explains why amenability belongs to large-scale geometry. The recurring visual test is boundary compared with volume.
